text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--The first goods train went through the tunnel section of the Great Belt road-rail, tunnel-bridge fixed link under the waterway between Denmark's two biggest islands inaugurating the country's biggest engineering project ever. The eight km journey took five minutes. In June the link opens for passenger trains, with private cars following in summer 1998 when the eastern suspension bridge is completed, linking Zealand on which Copenhagen stands and Funen with the mainland.

--Prime minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen insists that Denmark's support of Baltic state Latvia's wish to join NATO and the European Union remains unchanged despite the deletion of references to the matter in a banquet speech by Queen Margrethe to visiting Latvian president Guntis Ulmanis.

--Renewed pressure is being brought on Denmark to toe the line and participate in joint European Union legal and police cooperation. A draft future EU treaty document by the Dutch presidency calls for these aspects to be incorporated in union institutions. Denmark opted out of joint EU legal and police cooperation in a Maastricht Treaty referendum in 1993.
--Danish companies are gradually giving in to pressure to increase dividends. 1996 corporate results show a new tendency for bigger dividends for shareholders.
--Den Danske Bank, Denmark's biggest bank, is to close its telephone discount bank in three months time with the 10,000 private clients' accounts to be transferred to the main bank.

--The deficit in NKT Holding's troubled vacuum cleaner unit Nilfisk was halved to 97 million crowns in 1996 due to a good performance by its U.S. subsidiary but management said it was still very dissatisfied with the result.

--74 percent of Denmark's captains of industry support former foreign minister and present Liberal Party leader Uffe Ellemann-Jensen as candidate to be the next Danish prime minister, according to a survey.
--Danish shipping risks political pressure if the number of Danish seamen employed in the Danish commercial fleet continues to fall drastically.
